title: You can’t tickle yourself because your brain predicts the touch
body: In 1998, Sarah-Jayne Blakemore and colleagues used brain imaging to study the self-tickle response. When volunteers used a joystick to control a small tickling robot themselves, they could not make themselves laugh. The explanation: the **cerebellum**, which helps coordinate movement, sends the somatosensory cortex precise information about where your own movement will land, and a cortical mechanism, still not fully identified, then damps the sensation. Another person’s fingers can’t be forecast, so the full surprise arrives on your skin.

slides.heading: Why self-tickling fails
items: You decide to move your hand
The cerebellum predicts the touch and tells the somatosensory cortex
That predicted sensation is damped, so it barely registers
Another person’s hand can’t be predicted: full tickle

slides.prompt: In 1897, psychologists G. Stanley Hall and Arthur Allin split tickling into two kinds. What are they called?
slides.detail: Knismesis is the light, moving itch; gargalesis the harsher, deeper pressure that makes you laugh.

left.label: Knismesis
left.text: A mildly annoying sensation caused by a light movement on the skin, like an insect crawling.

right.label: Gargalesis
right.text: A laughter-provoking feeling from harsher, deeper pressure. Thought limited to humans and other primates, and perhaps rats.

slides.heading: Robots and rats
slides.text: In another experiment, people laughed just as much when they believed a machine was tickling them as when they thought a person was. And some research indicates that rats can be tickled too.
